title: Dynamic Risk Assessment for Oil and Gas Resource Countries Using an Optimized SVM Model
affiliations: China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) - PetroChina

detail.title: Dynamic Risk Assessment for Oil and Gas Resource Countries Using an Optimized SVM Model
detail.abstract: This paper constructs a scientific and systematic risk assessment index system tailored for oil and gas resourceendowed countries, with a rigorous screening process yielding 46 valid indicators categorized into five core dimensions: political risk, economic risk, operational environment risk, oil and gas industry risk, and the China-specific factors. These dimensions comprehensively cover the macro policy environment, micro market operation conditions, and bilateral cooperation characteristics that affect Chinese overseas oil and gas investment decisions. On this basis, a support vector machine (SVM) model is established to quantitatively assess and rank the investment risks of 36 key oil and gas resource countries that host Chinese direct investment, leveraging the SVM model’s superior performance in handling small-sample, non-linear, and high-dimensional data. Finally, in-depth case studies on Canada and Sudan are con-ducted, with the two countries representing different types of oil and gas investment destinations in terms of economic development level and geopolitical background, thus fully verifying the feasibility, efficiency, and applicability of the proposed index system and assessment model.

title: Epistemology and Foundations of Ecological Macroeconomic Modeling: From off-Rooted Utility Value to a Negentropy-Based Metric

detail.title: Epistemology and Foundations of Ecological Macroeconomic Modeling: From off-Rooted Utility Value to a Negentropy-Based Metric

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interest
declarations.funderStatement: No fund received

detail.abstract: Ecological macroeconomic modeling faces a foundational difficulty that is epistemological before being technical: modern macroeconomics typically evaluates production and progress through a utility-value metric (prices, GDP, welfare equivalents) that is consistent inside an anthropocentric framework composed of free agents. But it remains off rooted from reservoirs and sinks, the biophysical and social containers that make production possible and that absorb its degradation. The result is a systematic asymmetry, between market economics, inconsistently closed, and natural and social prerequisites to any activity, generating “externalities.” This paper proposes a thermodynamics-inspired epistemic reconstruction. Building on Georgescu-Rogen’s entropy-law critique of economic circularity and Daly’s operational rules of sustainability, the macroeconomy is reframed as a dissipative structure that mobilizes reservoirs of negentropy (natural and social capital) and rejects entropy into sinks (pollution). The paper then argues that the missing ingredient is not “substitutability” per se, but a universal metric that makes different forms of capital, natural and social, comparable. Then, the article proposes a metric for the natural and social capital, equivalent (up to a scale factor) to a negentropy, and which combines the thermodynamic (Clausius), material (Georgescu-Roegen), and informational (Shannon) entropies. Finally, as in thermodynamics for energy, the introduction of a conservation principle makes sustainability measurable and enforceable within macroeconomic modeling and accounting.

title: How Extreme Are America’s Electoral Maps? A Tail Probability Test for Gerrymandering

detail.title: How Extreme Are America’s Electoral Maps? A Tail Probability Test for Gerrymandering

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
How extreme are American electoral maps in practice? This question is answered with a party-symmetric probability diagnostic that converts observed vote-seat outcomes into a one-sided tail probability under a transparent multinomial null distribution (implemented via its binomial marginal). The extremeness statistic is reported on an unbounded log-odds scale, enabling direct comparison across states, chamber sizes, and election windows and allowing persistence to accumulate across cycles rather than being compressed on a bounded index. Additional extremeness tests based on Hoeffding's inequality and the beta-binomial distribution are considered as supplements.

In U.S. House delegations (2022-2024), the most extreme states under this baseline are California, Illinois, Tennessee, Maryland, and New Jersey, while Pennsylvania, Michigan, Minnesota, Colorado, and Virginia are the least extreme. In state lower chambers (2021-2025), Oklahoma, West Virginia, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Hawaii are the most extreme, while Minnesota, Michigan, Georgia, Montana, and New Hampshire are the least extreme.

It is likely that political party strength, institutional constraints, and entrenchment incentives substantially influence how statewide support translates into durable seat dominance - and serve as an explanation for extremeness heterogeneity. And when outcomes persist in the tail of a stated reference distribution, a benign explanation becomes increasingly strained.

title: Is the Economy a Lyving Structure?

detail.title: Is the Economy a Lyving Structure?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interest

detail.abstract: This article defends an economy that should not merely be compared to a living system but understood as one in an analytical and ontological sense. Built on thermodynamics, a recent definition of life defines living systems as dissipative structures characterized by autocatalysis, homeostasis, and learning (written "Lyfe" to distinguish from biological definition). The article demonstrates that society and the economy fulfill these criteria. By reframing economic dynamics within this natural framework, it opens new explanations for growth and crises, and sets up sustainability as an endogenous property of the economy. It offers new analytical foundations for understanding economic instability and long-term viability.

affiliations: Ghent University - Department of Economics, Swedish Public Employment Service, Ghent University - Department of Personnel Management, Work and Organizational Psychology, Swedish Public Employment Service and Uppsala University

detail.title: Motivating Job Seekers. A Field Experiment
detail.abstract: Reduced motivation among jobseekers over the unemployment spell may lead to declining job-finding rates. We report findings from a low-cost digital intervention with motivational emails aimed at enhancing and sustaining motivation and search effort among job seekers in Sweden. Using a randomized controlled trial that included 200,720 job seekers, we evaluate both carrot messages aimed at encouraging the pursuit of personal goals and intrinsic motivation and stick messages focusing on external pressure and constraints. A large share of job seekers opened the emails, and they triggered behavioral responses. Both types of messages backfired, reducing search effort and job-finding rates. The carrot messages reduced both the number of job applications and job finding, particularly among men. One likely explanation is that these messages signal to job seekers that the Public Employment Service was less controlling than initially perceived, prompting a reduction in effort. The stick messages backfired for job seekers who, at the onset of unemployment, reported that they were motivated by an inner drive rather than by constraints. These findings underscore the challenges of motivating job seekers to actively search for jobs and suggest that low-cost digital interventions, in isolation, are inadequate and may even be counterproductive.

title: CreditSentinel AI: An ML-Augmented Credit Risk Framework for Emerging Markets
affiliations: NMIMS Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering

detail.title: CreditSentinel AI: An ML-Augmented Credit Risk Framework for Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: Traditionally, the process of credit risk adjudication has relied on periodic financial disclosures, supplemented with heuristic-based analyses. Although the process offers some level of oversight, the approach has significant drawbacks, such as information latency and cognitive bias. These issues are further compounded by the nature of the markets, which are known to be volatile, with opaque financial disclosures and significant governance risks. In the present research, the authors introduce CreditSentinel AI, a high-quality, machine learning-based approach to solvency analysis. The proposed CreditSentinel AI model utilizes non-linear eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), incorporating high-frequency market data and fundamental financial statement-based financial information. The key differentiator of the CreditSentinel AI approach is the Graduated Penalty Mechanism (GPM), which utilizes severity-weighted risk adjustments, as opposed to binary covenant-based risk adjustments. In the proposed research, the CreditSentinel AI approach was tested using stress tests on listed firms on the National Stock Exchange (NSE), demonstrating the proposed approach's capability to detect structurally distressed capital profiles and leverage-based default risks. CreditSentinel AI has the potential to become a high-performance, automated first-line risk sentinel, capable of reducing decision latency.

detail.abstract: When a person reports an experience that exceeds available frameworks for verification-captivity, transcendence, contact with something genuinely other-the clinical system must respond. That response is shaped by forces that may have little to do with truth: billing codes, diagnostic categories without biomarkers, insurance protocols, and a longstanding institutional discomfort with the unknown, frequently dressed as scientific rigor. This paper applies the Coordination Invariant (S = C/V) to the psychiatric encounter. The core argument: what gets labeled "crazy" is not always a medical determination. It may be a coordination failure. The patient arrives with high interpretive variance and minimal shared constraint. The clinician operates inside a system that requires a category. The system integrates the person into its structure. The outcome is not always treatment. It is sometimes translation-from unverifiable witness to diagnostic code. And that translation, in some cases, functions as erasure.

title: Technical Note Three: The Horizon Scan From V = 0 – Compositional Opacity And Catastrophic Risk Under Quantum Integration

detail.title: Technical Note Three: The Horizon Scan From V = 0 – Compositional Opacity And Catastrophic Risk Under Quantum Integration

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.ethicsApproval: None.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded.

detail.abstract:
This technical note extends the "Governing AI Without Killing Value" series with a horizon stress-test: what happens when decision velocity increases faster than governance can verify. Technical Note One formalised the internal liability calculus under V = 0. Technical Note Two explained the market equilibrium that drives reliance drift. This note adds acceleration by treating quantum integration as a computational vector, not an intelligence claim. The verification constraint remains. The assurance window collapses.

It introduces the central expression V = 0 × Q → Cr and defines the conditions under which quantum-assisted optimisation or simulation converts structural verification absence into catastrophic risk (Cr) – the loss of the conditions required for an institution to function as intended. The argument is closed by three propositions: the risk is structural, it does not require sentience and it cannot be resolved by scaling computational capability alone.

The mechanism is grounded in precedent rather than futurism. The collapses of Barings (1995) and Long-Term Capital Management (1998) demonstrate that optimisation operating beyond verification discipline can produce catastrophic failure without intelligence, intent or malevolence. Quantum integration replicates those conditions at scale and speed, whilst introducing a new governance hazard class: floating provenance – the inability to reconstruct decision logic to an audit-grade standard inside the decision horizon because the causal path is not stable, replayable or independently reproducible within the assurance window.

The instruments do not change. The margin for error does. The note concludes with three board-operable requirements for any system incorporating quantum processing components before it enters high-consequence pathways: mandatory quantum-architecture disclosure, operational error-rate and coherence reporting and explicit floating-provenance classification within AI risk registers, with board-authorised constraint where standard assurance assumptions no longer hold.

detail.abstract:
This companion paper extends "Governing AI Without Killing Value" (White Paper) into third-party governance. It applies the same constraint – verification absent by construction (V = 0) and defensibility under compelled reconstruction – to consultancies, assurance providers and systems integrators.

Third-party comfort is not verification. Under V = 0 conditions, organisations respond to verification absence by hiring consultancies and assurance providers to “govern” what they cannot verify internally. The problem is structural: advisors face the same architectural constraint as the systems they are engaged to govern. They cannot manufacture decision-level verification artefacts that the underlying architecture does not produce. Yet organisations routinely treat advisory engagement as verification, comfort opinions as evidence, readiness assessments as assurance and sign-off as risk transfer. That is accountability arbitrage by proxy: the comfort is outsourced, the liability is not.

This paper maps the resulting Consultancy Dependency Cascade and specifies the enforcement architecture required to prevent advisory relationships becoming governance liabilities. It defines five instruments: (1) the Consultancy Dependency Cascade diagnostic, (2) a binding Board Mandate for authority preservation and the Evidence Supremacy Rule, (3) the External Assurance Test with a mandatory four-gate audit committee protocol, (4) a Consultancy Dependency Red-Flag Scorecard to stage drift in live engagements and (5) an Upstream Liability Evidence Preservation Protocol to preserve recovery optionality when scrutiny arrives. These instruments are designed to plug directly into the Sovereign Intelligence Flywheel enforcement model defined in the white paper.

The governing principle is blunt: mandated assurance is not mandated verification. Governance anchored in third-party reassurance creates a recursive disclaimer structure where vendors disclaim outputs, advisors disclaim verification and assurance providers disclaim liability beyond narrow scopes, while the board retains fiduciary, regulatory and litigation exposure. This paper replaces reassurance with reconstructability: "If the consultants disengaged today, could the organisation still explain and defend the decision without them?" If not, the engagement has become a governance dependency, not a control.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.ethicsApproval: None.

detail.abstract:
This companion supports the White Paper "Governing AI Without Killing Value" series by moving outside the organisation’s boundary. Technical Note One formalises the internal liability calculus: exposure forms when Reliance (R) rises under V = 0 without independent verification, then residual exposure is bounded by Governance, Accountability and Transparency (G + A + T). This note explains why reliance rises even when policy says it should not.

It defines the market equilibrium under V = 0: external actors are structurally incentivised to raise reliance without supplying external verification (Ve) or guaranteeing Pack Producibility (P). Confidence is commercially supplied whilst verification remains architecturally absent. The equilibrium is sustained by a recursive disclaimer structure: vendors disclaim outputs and reliance, advisors disclaim verification, assurance providers disclaim scope and the regulated entity retains all fiduciary, regulatory and litigation consequence.

The note introduces three environmental variables that sit outside direct organisational control but can be identified, measured and countered through internal governance: Vendor Pressure (Vp), Assurance Substitution (As) and Regulatory Scrutiny Intensity (Sc). It then shows how reliance drift becomes the default outcome unless governance counterforce is strong enough to hold R flat before Sc arrives.

A simple heuristic is provided for risk and audit teams: ΔR/Δt = f(I + Vp + As − (G + A + T)), where internal incentive pressure (I) combines with external headwinds unless governance counterforce is strong enough to make reliance drift non-positive before scrutiny arrives.

This note is analytical rather than instrumental. It explains why the existing instruments in the white paper and companion papers must be strong enough to resist the market. It includes variable-to-instrument mapping (Vp, As, Sc) to concrete controls and evidence capture requirements and a visual equilibrium model showing the binary outcome when Sc triggers the P test: P = 1 (reconstruction, upstream disclaimers irrelevant) versus P = 0 (crystallisation, organisation stands alone).

If you remember one insight: the market does not sell verification. It sells confidence. They are not the same thing.

detail.abstract:
This technical note supports the white paper series “Governing AI Without Killing Value” by formalising the liability mechanics beneath the KEV governance architecture. It extends the KEV baseline by adding a human governance variable, Reliance (R): exposure forms when organisations treat V = 0 outputs as provisionally reliable at the point of decision without independent verification.

The note is tiered for use. Tier 1 is board-operable and reduces the problem to a governance heuristic: V = 0 is the condition, R is the choice, Exposure is the result. Tier 2 makes governance proportionate by consequence and delegation, introducing Consequence (C) and Delegation (D), then centres the failure test decision Pack producibility (P): if scrutiny arrived tomorrow, can the organisation produce a reconstructable decision pack (P = 1)? Tier 3 adds optional diagnostics for risk and audit teams, including external verification strength (Ve), reliance drift (dR/dt), memory decay (M), source integrity (S), incentive pressure (I) and hygiene controls (H).

This is a governance heuristic, not a unit-based equation. Its purpose is to make reliance visible and defensibility executable, so unpriced exposure does not accumulate invisibly until a regulator, court, auditor, insurer or counterparty compels reconstruction. The note also includes a variable-to-instrument mapping that links each exposure driver to the relevant governing instruments across the white paper and companion controls.

title: Redefining Trash into Treasure: A Case Study of Guwahati's Waste Recycling Economy
affiliations: Independent, Gauhati University and Gauhati University

detail.title: Redefining Trash into Treasure: A Case Study of Guwahati's Waste Recycling Economy
detail.abstract: Globally, as cities grow at an accelerated rate, urban waste management has turned into a crucial challenge. Rapidly urbanising cities such as Guwahati in northeast India face unprecedented volumes of municipal solid waste (MSW) due to accelerating rate of waste generation and population growth. Driven by the impact of MSW on greenhouse gas emissions, the clustering of waste poses a significant risk to human health and disrupts local ecosystem while intensifying climate change. Being an innovative approach, the circular economy offers a promising solution to address these challenges as a closed-loop system in which resources are continuously cycled through the economy. An attempt has been made to understand the role of a local recycling plant in Guwahati in converting waste into resources in view of the circular economy. To conduct this study purposive sampling technique has been used and to collect first-hand data a semi-structured questionnaire has been prepared to carry out informal interviews along with Focus Group Discussion (FGD) and direct observation. For the analysis, this study adopts a qualitative descriptive approach. Moreover, this study sheds light on adopting effective sustainable waste management at the grassroots level, redefining waste from a societal burden into a treasure, leading to a greener, resource-efficient future for other cities.

detail.abstract: We develop a dynamic model in which firms choose debt to finance investment while facing collateral constraints and interest subsidies that reduce borrowing costs. The model predicts that subsidies increase leverage through cost, collateral, and expectations channels. Using the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act as a natural experiment, we find the opposite: treated semiconductor firms reduce leverage relative to control firms, with no change in debt issuance or borrowing costs. These results are consistent with dynamic capital structure models in which firms preserve financial flexibility when anticipating future investment needs and uncertainty in subsidy implementation.

title: Collusive Content in Corporate Communications
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania and

detail.title: Collusive Content in Corporate Communications
detail.abstract: In industries such as airlines, steel, and truck rentals, firms have coordinated to raise prices or reduce capacities using public announcements such as earnings calls. As this type of coordinating practice is relatively unexplored, this study seeks to learn more about the collusive content in firms' public communications. To do so, we design a large language model (LLM) to look for such content and then apply it to almost 500,000 company transcripts. The LLM is very selective in that only .12% of the transcripts satisfy the criterion for collusive content. The LLM is reasonably effective at rediscovering previously documented episodes and identifies many new episodes. A human audit is conducted of the 301 transcripts with the highest LLM scores. The audit distills and organizes the content to identify systematic ways in which it is facilitating coordinated conduct. Messages fall into two broad bins. First, a firm states that the industry needs to raise prices, reduce supply, or reduce capacity. Second, a firm expresses how it has been less aggressive and calls on competitors to join them, either explicitly or implicitly by saying it is "acting as a leader", commending rival firms who have acted in a similar manner, or criticizing rival firms that have not. A second research objective is to develop a screening tool for competition agencies and plaintiff law firms. Towards that end, the human audit evaluates the performance of the LLM in substituting for human experts. The LLM is capable of identifying a wide variety of collusive content though there is a reasonably high false positive rate. Nevertheless, we explain how it can be an essential component of a screening protocol and show proof of concept with a case study of the Brazilian domestic airline industry.

detail.abstract:
Case studies. Not theory. This companion to “Governing AI Without Killing Value” shows what liability looks like when verification is absent by construction (V = 0) and evidence is demanded. 

It applies the KEV framework and the AI Dependency Cascade to forensic reconstructions across regulated sectors. Each case isolates the decision points that matter: what authority was delegated, what assumptions were imported, what verification was performed and what could not be reconstructed later. Every case ends at the governance boundary – the moment a regulator, auditor, court, investor, ombudsman or customer compels reconstruction and the organisation discovers it cannot provide it. 

The intent is evidential scaffolding. Boards, executives, audit teams and regulators can use these reconstructions to pressure-test operating models, assurance design and board-level attestations. It is designed to support hostile diligence against current deployments and to specify procurement and assurance requirements that do not confuse prompt discipline with verification. If you can reconstruct the decision under force, you have governance. If you cannot, you have theatre. 

Case studies included:

  • A bank that loses the ability to explain its own risk under prudential scrutiny
  • A government department that cannot account for its own actions under judicial review
  • An insurer whose reserving trail collapses under audit and supervisory examination
  • A frontier AI lab forced into a >$600m impairment after customers cannot deploy under scrutiny
  • A VC diligence failure where AI validates AI, producing synthetic consensus and regulatory exposure
  • A software scale-up that loses reconstructability of its own codebase, then fails under incident pressure 

This companion and the wider publication series do not replace independent legal, regulatory or technical advice. They are built to make those discussions harder to wave away and easier to evidence.

title: Judgment Insolvency and the Matthew Gradient under AI Amplification
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Judgment Insolvency and the Matthew Gradient under AI Amplification

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the owner of the domain matthewgradient.com, which discusses related conceptual material. No external funding or financial sponsorship influenced this research.

detail.abstract: This paper reframes AI adoption in knowledge work as a problem of evaluative capacity rather than model capability. Standard productivity frameworks implicitly assume that value is constrained by generation: as models improve, human workload should decline and throughput should increase. We argue that this framing becomes structurally mis-specified when AI functions primarily as a throughput amplifier. As candidate generation approaches computational scale, the binding constraint shifts from production to entropy management-the ability to detect and suppress epistemic error, intent misalignment, and integration failure embedded in generated outputs. We formalize this shift through a judgment insolvency condition in which induced evaluative demand exceeds available judgment capacity. Because each generated candidate carries latent entropy, amplification increases not only output volume but total verification burden. When candidate throughput exceeds review bandwidth, overload is absorbed not through reduced commitment but through degraded evaluation depth. This mechanism explains the emergence of "workslop": outputs that inflate completion metrics while imposing hidden downstream integration costs. The model yields several counterintuitive implications. First, improvements in baseline model accuracy do not necessarily reduce total evaluative demand. As overt factual errors decline, residual failures concentrate in intent misalignment and near-miss errors that are more cognitively expensive to detect. Second, amplification generates divergence across organizations. Environments with high judgment quality can sustain greater throughput before entering insolvency, while low-judgment environments experience coordination overload at modest amplification levels. We term this regime-dependent divergence the Matthew Gradient. The framework implies that sustainable AI deployment requires throughput governance rather than output maximization. The central managerial problem is not accelerating generation, but aligning amplification with evaluative capacity under entropy-bearing production.

detail.abstract: Central bank liquidity backstops alter the incentives of money market funds (MMFs) by affecting the expected costs of liquidity management and redemption pressure. The Contingent Nonbank Repo Facility (CNRF), introduced in early 2025, was designed as a targeted liquidity support mechanism for nonbank financial institutions (NBFIs). Using high-frequency portfolio data, we show that Sterling-denominated MMFs rebalanced sharply toward riskier private assets following the facility's announcement-despite no signs of actual fund outflows. This reallocation coincided with declines in daily and weekly liquid asset buffers and a rise in portfolio maturity, consistent with increased risktaking under the protection of a prospective central bank backstop. We interpret these findings as consistent with moral hazard, where the expectation of support weakens incentives to self-insure against redemptions. Our findings contribute to understanding the unintended consequences of extending lender-of-last-resort functions to NBFIs.

title: A Super-Invention Taxonomy Extended to Genus Homo: Quantitative Hierarchical Analysis of Creative Output Across ~2.8 Million Years, Ending at the Sapiens-Only Transition (~41,500 BCE)
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Super-Invention Taxonomy Extended to Genus Homo: Quantitative Hierarchical Analysis of Creative Output Across ~2.8 Million Years, Ending at the Sapiens-Only Transition (~41,500 BCE)

declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
This working paper extends the author’s previously published Linnaean-style taxonomic model of humankind’s creative output — now termed super-inventions — across the genus Homo. Using strict criteria (durable, massively used, man-made opportunities delivering significant quality improvement over baseline), we classify super-inventions and classes of super-inventions produced by all members of the genus Homo from the point when members of the genus Homo became tool-making species, ~2.8 million years ago, until ~41,500 BCE, the point at which Homo sapiens became the sole surviving species.

The analysis is based on evidence of human creative actions, as described in research papers by multiple scholars. The results in this article present the shape, rate, and details of the genus Homo's development. Multiple inflection points were identified on the curve of a quantitative historical trajectory of the genus Homo's development.

The data reveal unambiguously directional accumulation of super-inventions throughout the ~2.8-million-year span. Multiple extinct Homo species demonstrably produced H-creative (historically novel, per Margaret Boden) super-inventions long before Homo sapiens existed or became the sole survivor.

Monte Carlo simulations of class misassignments yield error rates averaging 15.1% (standard deviation 8.3%) and a 95% confidence interval of 0–31.6%, comparable to biological taxonomy.

This paper provides an empirical baseline spanning ~2.8 million years for studying the genus Homo as a single system and directly supports the forthcoming The State of Sapiens Report book.

title: Conditional Belonging among Thai Indians: Everyday Boundary-Making through Lived Narratives

detail.title: Conditional Belonging among Thai Indians: Everyday Boundary-Making through Lived Narratives

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This article is primarily based on a critical integrative review of published literature. In addition, illustrative anecdotal material is drawn from a small set of previously collected reflective responses used solely for conceptual illustration. These responses were collected via an anonymised questionnaire, and no directly or indirectly identifiable personal data were retained. Informed consent to participate was obtained from all participants at the time of data collection. The collection, storage, and use of the anonymised responses were conducted in accordance with the principles of the Thailand Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), including data minimisation, purpose limitation, and protection of participant anonymity. Given the review-led nature of the article, the use of fully anonymised data, and the absence of sensitive personal information, formal institutional ethics committee approval was not required for this study.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors received no financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.

detail.abstract:
This article examines the experiences of Thai Indians as a long-settled population of migrant origin in Thailand, focusing on everyday belonging, ethnic boundary-making, and family-mediated inclusion in a South–South context. While Indian mobility to Thailand has often been examined through frameworks of expatriation, adjustment, or professional migration, far less attention has been paid to Thai Indians who are citizens of Thailand yet continue to negotiate recognition, legitimacy, and ethnic difference across generations. Drawing on a critical integrative review of peer-reviewed scholarship spanning foundational and contemporary debates in migration, diaspora, and ethnicity studies, and complemented by anonymised illustrative case narratives drawn from prior research materials, this article synthesises insights across sociology, migration studies, and South Asian diaspora research.

The analysis demonstrates that integration among Thai Indians is neither linear nor complete. Despite long-term settlement, linguistic competence, intermarriage, and formal citizenship, belonging frequently remains conditional and situational, shaped by visible difference, language accent, religious practice, and family configurations. The analysis highlights family and gender as central yet under-theorised mechanisms through which ethnic boundaries are reproduced, softened, or reworked in everyday life. Marriage patterns, spousal nationality, intergenerational educational strategies, and women’s roles as cultural brokers emerge as key sites where belonging is actively negotiated.

By reframing Thai Indians not as expatriates or assimilating migrants but as a migrant-origin population embedded within Thailand’s social fabric, this article challenges assimilationist assumptions that equate cultural adaptation with social inclusion. It contributes to scholarly debates by advancing a family-centred, gender-aware understanding of conditional belonging and by extending theories of ethnicity, boundary-making, and citizenship into a South–South migration context.

detail.abstract:
This report marks our 3rd year of tracking the growth and development of online alternative finance industry in the Asia Pacific region. Our report last year reflected how this nascent industry has evolved across the region, affecting the way people, businesses and institutions access, raise and invest money. This year’s report illustrates the geographically uneven yet considerable growth of online alternative finance in many countries across the Asia Pacific region. detail.abstract: Organisational Factors play a central role in shaping work systems and determining occupational safety and health outcomes; however, existing evidence remains fragmented and largely concentrated in specific industrial sectors. This study aims to systematically identify, validate, and prioritise Organisational Factors influencing occupational safety in work systems, with particular attention to the food retail sector, an operationally complex and underrepresented service context. An integrated methodological design was adopted, combining a PRISMA-based systematic literature review with an expert-based Delphi study. The systematic review identified 52 Organisational Factors reported across 34 empirical studies, which were subsequently harmonised to ensure conceptual consistency. These factors were organised into nine thematic groups and subjected to expert validation and prioritisation through two Delphi rounds. The process resulted in a final validated framework comprising 68 Organisational Factors distributed across nine domains. The evaluation phase revealed marked differences in the perceived impact of organisational domains, with Safety Climate and Employee Development achieving the highest mean impact scores. Training emerged as the most influential individual factor, followed by safety behaviours and compliance, and the provision of safety equipment. The findings confirm the systemic and multidimensional nature of occupational safety and highlight the importance of integrated organisational approaches, particularly in service-based environments such as food retail. This study provides a robust conceptual and operational foundation to further development of organisational safety strategies and to promote future research.

title: The Ownership Gap - Digital Capital and the Structure of Economic Recognition

detail.title: The Ownership Gap - Digital Capital and the Structure of Economic Recognition
detail.abstract:
This paper identifies and analyzes a structural condition in contemporary capital formation termed the ownership gap: the divergence between those who materially contribute to the formation of durable capital systems and those who hold residual ownership claims over the resulting assets.

The argument proceeds in four stages. First, it examines how codification, persistent measurement, and large-scale aggregation transform distributed human participation into formative input at the capital formation stage — a threshold at which activity becomes asset without altering ownership. Second, it identifies two engines that drive this divergence: automation without continuity, which transfers accumulated expertise from human actors into owned infrastructure, and participation as infrastructure, which converts ongoing human activity into the substrate of durable capital systems. Third, it evaluates why the policy instruments most commonly proposed in response,  competition enforcement, income redistribution, and consent mechanisms — are structurally downstream of the formation stage and do not address the origin of asymmetry. Fourth, it introduces the Human-Derived Capital Trust as a directional institutional construct demonstrating that ownership recognition at the formation stage is conceivable within existing legal traditions.

The ownership gap is distinguished from adjacent arguments concerning wage suppression, market concentration, and behavioral surveillance. It is an architectural condition, embedded at the moment capital forms and is shown to compound over time through persistence, irreversibility, and intergenerational transmission of ownership claims. The paper argues that ownership categories, which have historically evolved in response to shifts in capital formation logic, may require recalibration under contemporary conditions of digital capital accumulation.

detail.abstract: In light of the Madoff case, we present an Agent-Based Model of a Ponzi scheme. Agents are initially inclined to invest in the scam because they believe the wealth will increase, even if the fraudster dissipates it without any investment. We stress that the main characteristic of such schemes is the growing discrepancy between the perceived wealth and the actual total amount of money in the impostor's possession. The tendency gradually reverses and more agents withdraw their wealth (and made-up profits) if trust is lost as a result of hearing negative news about the economy. We look at how long it takes to expose the fraud and file for bankruptcy in relation to the volume of news that enters the market. We also look into the impact of a special agent dubbed Markopolos (inspired by a genuine personage) on the time to bankruptcy because of his capacity to quickly "convince" the agents he encounters to disinvest. Although the Markopolos effect seems to be statistically significant, it is not very strong when it comes to the results of a news flow and the subsequent widespread loss of faith and redemptions.

detail.title: Traffic Assignment as a Differentiable Program
detail.abstract: Differentiable programming enables the efficient computation of gradients for complex mathematical models via automatic differentiation. In this note, we examine its application to transportation research by recasting traffic assignment as a differentiable program that can be embedded within broader hierarchical optimization and learning frameworks. Differentiable traffic assignment (DiTA) replaces conventional equilibrium conditions with an "equilibrium generation" process that is both smooth and behaviorally grounded. This reformulation allows modelers to assess how assignment outcomes respond to changes in input parameters by differentiating through the equilibrium generation process, effectively performing backpropagation, in the language of neural networks. By leveraging the computational infrastructure developed for training neural networks, DiTA has the potential to transform the way a wide range of transportation problems, particularly those formulated as bi-level programs, are solved. This note presents the conceptual foundations of DiTA, discusses key implementation challenges, and highlights promising future directions.

detail.abstract: The residential sector is one of the largest consumers of energy, contributing significantly to climate change. Understanding the energy behaviour of households can allow policymakers design more effective targeted policies, achieving the targets of net-zero emissions. We analyse the drivers of electricity and gas expenditure among low-income households using an administrative panel dataset of housing benefit recipients for 2018-2023. These results are compared to the energy expenditure of average households using the EU-SILC dataset. We employ the adaptive Lasso for covariate selection and estimate a panel fixed effects model separately for homeowners and renters, motivated by the tenant-landlord problem. Electricity and gas have similar determinants, but gas expenditure is generally more elastic, reacting more to household composition and prices. Homeowners respond more to income and social benefits, while renters are more price-sensitive, by about 3-5%. Low-income households are considerably more vulnerable to price shocks and energy poverty than the average households. The counterfactuals indicate that low-income household energy spending would have been 15-20% lower in the absence of the energy crisis, while VAT cuts offer limited effectiveness. Our results highlight the need for policies that combine targeted energy rebates for low-income households and strong incentives for landlords to upgrade housing, to satisfy both affordability and national climate objectives.

title: GARP: Generalized Adaptive Rank Portfolio A Crisis-Adaptive, Assumption-Free Framework for Portfolio Construction

detail.title: GARP: Generalized Adaptive Rank Portfolio A Crisis-Adaptive, Assumption-Free Framework for Portfolio Construction
detail.abstract:
Portfolio construction has a unification problem. Mean-variance optimisation, Black-Litterman, and Hierarchical Risk Parity each solve part of the allocation problem while imposing their own distributional assumptions, methodological constraints, and arbitrary design choices. No existing framework simultaneously admits a freely chosen return signal, a freely chosen risk measure, a freely chosen crisis indicator, and a crisis-adaptive allocation mechanism without distributional assumptions.

This paper introduces GARP (Generalized Adaptive Rank Portfolio), a theoretical framework that resolves this fragmentation. GARP replaces Gaussian priors, heuristic bisection, and hard cluster assignments with a single continuous recursion through a crisis-adaptive asset hierarchy. At each node of the dendrogram, asset weights evolve as a product of three freely chosen rank scores - return attractiveness, risk, and tail contagion - scaled by marginal risk contribution and governed by a scalar crisis probability. Every input slot is free: any return signal, any risk measure, any tail dependence estimator, any crisis indicator is admissible.

The central result is a unification theorem: 1/N, IVP, ERC, HRP, HERC, and BL-HRP are all special cases of GARP under specific parameter choices. Four mathematical properties are proved: validity, continuity, crisis monotonicity, and degeneracy. Eight assumptions are stated explicitly with their roles, implications, and relaxation paths. Three concrete instantiations for global equities are fully specified to demonstrate modularity. Preliminary evidence from precursor models achieves a Sharpe ratio of 1.89 against a best benchmark of 0.22 and reduces the 2020 COVID peak drawdown by 75% relative to equal weighting. Full empirical evaluation across all three instantiations is the subject of a companion paper.

GARP is to portfolio construction what GARCH is to volatility modelling: not one more model, but the framework that contains them all.

title: Cavitation-Induced Hysteresis in Economic Networks: A Hydrodynamic Phase Transition Model of Operational Solvency

detail.title: Cavitation-Induced Hysteresis in Economic Networks: A Hydrodynamic Phase Transition Model of Operational Solvency
detail.abstract: Standard models of supply chain dynamics, specifically the "Bullwhip E ect," treat network nodes as elastic media subject to harmonic oscillation. This framework assumes that capacity is a continuous variable and that perturbations are reversible: when variance subsides, the system relaxes to equilibrium. We propose that this linear approximation holds only within laminar flow regimes and fails to account for topological phase transitions observed during high-amplitude volatility. Using a hydrodynamic isomorphism, we model the firm as a fluid conduit subject to thermodynamic constraints. We derive a critical threshold where local static pressure (𝑃 , representing liquidity) drops below the system's vapor pressure (𝑃 , representing fixed solvency requirements). Below this threshold, the node does not merely experience flow retardation; it undergoes a discrete phase transition from a liquid (operational) state to a vapor (insolvent) state. This transition introduces a "Capacity Void" and structural hysteresis, rendering the system non-ergodic over the recovery horizon. We introduce the Net Positive Solvency Head (𝑁𝑃𝑆𝐻) metric to quantify the metastability of the network node. Empirical validation against 2021 semiconductor supply data suggests that e iciency optimization (maximizing flow velocity 𝑣) systematically reduces the pressure margin, driving the system toward a critical point where minor stochastic fluctuations trigger catastrophic structural cavitation.

title: The Trust Tax: Cognitive Offloading In Supply Chain Mechanism Design

detail.title: The Trust Tax: Cognitive Offloading In Supply Chain Mechanism Design
detail.abstract: Global supply chain governance has failed because it ignores the constraints of Bounded Rationality. The current "Audit Society" generates high-entropy signals, voluminous certificates and site visits, that overwhelm the cognitive bandwidth of agents, forcing them to rely on "Defection" as a fast and frugal heuristic. We analyze the 2025 UFLPA crisis, where a 77% isotopic failure rate (U.S. Customs and Border Protection, 2025) exposed the decoupling of administrative maps from physical territory, creating a classic Incomplete Contract problem (Hart & Moore, 1990) where residual control rights are unenforceable. This paper proposes "Hamiltonian Mechanism Design" not merely as a contract, but as a Cognitive O loader. By mapping the biological primitive of eusocial policing (rB > C) to smart contracts via "Escrowed Latency" and "Isotopic Triangulation," we collapse complex trust decisions into a binary liquidity signal. This reduces the information processing cost of integrity, allowing agents to "satisfice" safely without the "moral wiggle room" (Dana et al., 2007) that currently facilitates systemic defection. We introduce the "Judas Protocol" to destabilize cartel cognition and "Integrity Staking Pools" to financialize reputation. We argue that the "Trust Tax" is a product of cognitive overload, and that shifting from ceremonial verification to algorithmic shared destiny aligns economic incentives with the limits of human cognition.

detail.abstract:
This research report, authored by Md Rashidul Hasan of the University of Waikato, investigates the economic impact of the dual technology transition—Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Clean-Tech—on corporate performance as of January 2026. Analyzing a panel dataset of 500 firms across five major industries (2021–2025), the study quantifies how technology adoption drives measurable improvements in Total Factor Productivity (TFP), profitability, and market valuation.

Key Findings
  • Productivity Drivers: Regression analysis shows that AI adoption has a strong positive impact on TFP with a coefficient of 0.329, meaning a 10-point increase in a firm's AI adoption score correlates to a 3.3% rise in TFP. Clean-tech adoption offers a complementary productivity channel with a coefficient of 0.190.
  • Valuation & Profitability Premiums: Technology leaders in the highest AI adoption quintile command an average Tobin’s Q of 2.00, representing a 22% valuation premium over laggards. High-AI firms also achieve a significantly higher Return on Equity (ROE) of 38.1% compared to 30.9% for low-AI firms.
  • Risk-Return Profiles: Contradicting conventional wisdom, higher technology adoption is associated with lower volatility (31.2% for high-AI vs. 35.6% for low-AI firms). High-technology portfolios deliver a Sharpe ratio of 1.08, a 46% improvement in risk-adjusted returns.
  • Industry Trends: The Technology sector leads in AI adoption (79.0) and valuation (2.13 Tobin's Q), while the Energy sector dominates in clean-tech adoption (82.0). Manufacturing shows a balanced approach, effectively integrating both technologies.

The report concludes that by 2026, technology investments have become strategic imperatives rather than discretionary expenses. Firms that successfully navigate the accelerating convergence of AI and Clean-Tech are positioned to define the next decade of competitive success and shareholder value creation.

detail.abstract: Legislative activity on AI governance has surged globally, yet we lack comparative empirical evidence on how "law hardening" develops and which pre-legislative activities catalyse binding regulation. We analyse the AI policy formation pipeline using more than 8,000 policy documents from 76 countries. Using Cox survival models, event studies, and Granger-style tests, we examine whether binding AI laws are driven by domestic pre-legislative activity or cross-border diffusion. We find that domestic accumulation of soft policy strongly predicts the timing of hard law adoption, while peer-country activity and other diffusion channels show no consistent effects. The observed trajectory reflects progressive, endogenous institutionalisation: strategic and discursive documents are followed by evidence production, then soft law adoption, and ultimately binding legislation. This pattern challenges accounts of performative policymaking in emerging technology regulation and suggests that soft law functions as an institutional stepping stone for learning and legitimation that catalyses subsequent hard law adoption.

detail.abstract:
Background: The global healthcare system operates predominantly in a reactive modepatients seek medical attention only after symptoms become clinically significant. This delay results in preventable mortality and morbidity across major disease categories including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, neurological disorders, and respiratory conditions. 

Objective: To propose a comprehensive, ethically grounded framework for AI-driven continuous health monitoring that enables early detection of disease-indicative physiological anomalies before clinical symptom onset. 

Methods: We conducted a narrative review of existing literature on wearable health monitoring, AI-based clinical diagnostics, federated learning for healthcare, and health notification systems. Based on identified evidence and gaps, we designed a four-layer system architecture comprising: 1. passive multimodal sensing, 2. data fusion and personalized baseline construction, 3. AI-based anomaly detection and risk scoring, and 4. tiered intelligent notification with care navigation integration. 

Results: We present a detailed system architecture incorporating wearable devices, smart home sensors, and smartphone-based passive monitoring. A personalized baseline approachcomputing individual Z-score deviations rather than population norms-is proposed to reduce false positives. Disease-specific detection models are outlined for six priority conditions. A phased four-stage research roadmap spanning ten years is described, with defined metrics for clinical validation. 

Conclusions: The convergence of ubiquitous sensing, advanced machine learning, and connectivity infrastructure creates a viable pathway toward proactive healthcare. The proposed framework addresses key gaps in existing systems including personalization, multimodal fusion, equity, and care integration. A structured research agenda is proposed to validate and deploy this framework at clinical and population scale.

detail.abstract: This study examines how On-site Adaptive Innovation (OAI) manifests differently in the semiconductor and robotics industries, using Abstractness and Control Structure as the main analytical dimensions. The semiconductor industry, characterized by high abstractness, addresses design–constraint conflicts through dual integration: horizontal heterogeneous integration of components (GPU, HBM, etc.) and vertical orchestration across the supply chain, with leadership shifting toward packaging-based integration capabilities. In contrast, the robotics industry, constrained by low abstractness and real-time safety requirements, achieves adaptivity through distributed control and middleware-centered cooperation within a tri-polar structure, where solution providers play a central role in knowledge assetization and orchestration. By comparing these pathways, the study highlights the symmetrical yet distinct mechanisms of OAI across industries and argues that future industrial leadership will depend not on single-product performance but on the assetization of field knowledge and intelligent IP.

title: Fundamental Dilemmas: Why Cognitive Security Cannot Be Absolute

detail.title: Fundamental Dilemmas: Why Cognitive Security Cannot Be Absolute
detail.abstract: Cognitive security confronts three structural dilemmas that can be neither ignored nor definitively resolved. The first sets the protection of the informational space against freedom of expression: any act of filtering or moderation entails a trade-off between censorship and vulnerability, with no objective threshold capable of resolving it. The second creates tension between defensive effectiveness and available resources: exhaustive verification is the theoretical gold standard, but its cognitive and economic cost renders it physically impossible at the scale of contemporary information flows. The third, perhaps the most fundamental, concerns the adversarial dynamic between defence and adaptation: any protection system creates a signature that attackers learn to circumvent, engaging an arms race with no stable end state. This article demonstrates that these three dilemmas are not independent-they feed one another in vicious cycles that render each partial attempt at resolution self-defeating. Faced with this reality, strategic maturity does not consist in seeking a non-existent optimal solution, but in composing defensive portfolios with complementary profiles, modulating equilibria according to threat levels, and investing in innovations capable of shifting the boundaries of the possible. Cognitive security is a process of continuous management, not a destination.

detail.abstract: Simulated phishing campaigns are among the most widely deployed tools for reducing organizational cyber risk. Yet the behavioral data these campaigns produce have an underappreciated structural feature and a resulting complication: because training is triggered by clicking, the very employees who receive intervention are those Teachable-moment design features also matter: emotion or heuristic framing and explicit reporting pitch can largely eliminate persistence, while annotated-email cues modestly exacerbate it. Finally, employees who engage with the education page still exhibit greater persistence than those who dismiss it, consistent with an emboldening mechanism in consequence-free training environments. We contribute to the IS security literature, methodologically, by integrating MSMs and CRE into a portable analytical framework that any organization with standard phishing-simulation platform logs can apply; and practically, by identifying specific education-design levers and strategies for managing a phishing-test paradox in organizations, so that they can more effectively design, sequence, and evaluate their simulated phishing programs.

title: Is There (Still) Anybody Out There? Online Forums in the Age of Generative AI
affiliations: and Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) - Faculty of Business Administration (Munich School of Management)

detail.title: Is There (Still) Anybody Out There? Online Forums in the Age of Generative AI
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is reshaping how individuals search for information and solve problems. For decades, online forums, particularly in technical and programming communities, have served as core infrastructure for decentralized knowledge production. We study how the diffusion of generative AI affects participation, question complexity, and solution quality in such communities, and whether governance structures moderate AI-driven substitution. Using a decade-long panel of posts and traffic data, we compare Statalist, a real-name forum, with pseudonymous platforms (Stack Overflow and Stack Exchange's Cross Validated) around the introduction of ChatGPT in November 2022. We combine activity measures with large-scale textual analyses, including an LLM-based complexity taxonomy and a benchmark comparison between community answers and a standardized "AI expert" proposal. We find that posting activity declines across platforms, but less sharply in the non-anonymous setting. At the same time, the share of high-complexity questions increases more strongly on Statalist, suggesting that AI primarily displaces routine problem solving while communities retain a comparative advantage in complex, context-rich discussions. However, more recent data indicate that this resilience may be transitional rather than permanent. Overall, our results suggest that governance shapes how the division of labor between humans and AI evolves in digital knowledge communities.

detail.abstract: The only study using nationally representative administrative records-tracking 25,000 workers across two years following the public release of ChatGPT-finds a confidence interval ruling out earnings effects larger than two percent, yet controlled experiments conducted over the same period report productivity improvements of 14 to 55 percent. Resolving this empirical paradox is the central aim of this systematic review and quantitative evidence synthesis of studies examining generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools and worker productivity. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines, a systematic search of six databases identified 60 records; after removing three duplicates, 57 unique records were screened, yielding 11 empirical studies spanning 2023 to 2026 with a combined participant total of 269,138. The sample-size-weighted mean productivity improvement was 20.9 percent. The observed range across positive-effect studies was 3.6 to 55.8 percent. Across six studies reporting experience-level moderation, 83 percent found greater gains for less experienced workers; the largest real-world observational study reversed this pattern specifically within production software development. A Task-Expertise-Measurement (TEM) Framework is proposed as a falsifiable candidate framework to reconcile observed heterogeneity, grounded in cognitive load theory and the expertise reversal effect, with seven falsifiable hypotheses advanced for the next research cycle.

title: Strategic AI Governance: Platform Adaptation to Regulatory and Competitive Constraints
affiliations: Astana IT University

detail.title: Strategic AI Governance: Platform Adaptation to Regulatory and Competitive Constraints
detail.abstract: This paper develops a conceptual framework for understanding how digital platforms adapt algorithmic governance in response to institutional and competitive constraints. Existing research has clarified how algorithmic systems influence platform accountability, bias, or control yet offers limited traction on how such systems are selectively modified as part of broader adaptive behavior. The Strategic AI Governance (SAIG) framework addresses this gap by analyzing algorithmic governance not as a static configuration but as a field of strategic adjustment. It identifies four governance domains-behavioral control, compliance signaling, market intermediation, and institutional positioning-through which platforms recalibrate AI systems to manage external demands while maintaining discretionary control. The SAIG model integrates behavioral, economic, and institutional perspectives to explain how algorithmic tools are used not only to optimize operations or signal compliance but to reorganize the conditions under which institutional constraints apply. Case illustrations from Google Play, Amazon Marketplace, and Meta's content governance demonstrate how these domains operate across different platform settings. Although the implementation varies, each case reflects a shared logic of adaptive governance that combines formal responsiveness with sustained control over rule enforcement and access. This framework contributes to platform governance research and ongoing debates on AI governance by clarifying how algorithmic systems are instrumentalized to navigate regulatory exposure and reinforce strategic advantage. It offers a basis for analyzing institutional responses to AIenabled governance and supports future inquiry into how different regulatory environments influence the elasticity of platform adjustment.

title: The Unowned Layer: Interpretation in AI-Assisted Decision Making

detail.title: The Unowned Layer: Interpretation in AI-Assisted Decision Making

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has filed a provisional patent application related to structured governance mechanisms for interpretive transformation described conceptually in this manuscript. No other financial or personal conflicts of interest are declared.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or identifiable personal information. Institutional review board approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence systems are now embedded in high-stakes institutional decision making. Governance frameworks have responded by strengthening model validation, bias mitigation, drift monitoring, documentation, and formal human oversight. These efforts address real technical and procedural risks. Yet one structural stage remains largely unexamined.

Between probabilistic computation and formal human approval lies a translation process. Statistical output is reformatted into scores, summaries, rankings, dashboards, and narratives. When uncertainty is converted into structured signals, the range of plausible interpretation narrows and perceived confidence can expand beyond what the evidence alone supports. In capital-intensive and regulated environments, this compression can influence resource allocation, shape regulatory posture, and build organizational momentum before the evidentiary base has materially changed.

Many AI-assisted failures are therefore neither computational errors nor lapses in responsibility. They arise from unexamined interpretive compression built into workflow design. Drawing on behavioral research and documented cases from regulated domains, this paper argues that interpretation should be treated as a distinct and governable stage in AI-assisted decision making. The next phase of AI oversight must address how probabilistic output becomes institutional meaning before authority is exercised, commitments are made, and capital or clinical momentum forms around conclusions that exceed the underlying evidence.

title: Fractal-cyclical Economic Time: A Multi-scale Framework for Understanding Long-run Development
affiliations: ACTAG

detail.title: Fractal-cyclical Economic Time: A Multi-scale Framework for Understanding Long-run Development
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework that reconceptualizes economic time as simultaneously fractal and cyclical, integrating insights from institutional economics, complexity theory, and historical analysis. I propose that economic development exhibits selfsimilar patterns across temporal scales from daily transactions to millennial transformations while simultaneously following cyclical rhythms at each scale. The framework synthesizes three theoretical traditions: Braudel's longue durée, North's institutional path dependence, and Mandelbrot's fractal geometry applied to markets. This synthesis generates testable propositions about how micro-level economic behaviors replicate macro-level institutional patterns, how different temporal cycles interact through scale-dependent feedback mechanisms, and why certain economies become locked into persistent development trajectories. The framework offers practical implications for development policy by suggesting that sustainable change requires alignment across temporal scales and that interventions must account for both the fractal replication of institutional patterns and the phase positions within multiple overlapping cycles.

title: When Standards Meet Patents: The Economics of SEPs and FRAND

detail.title: When Standards Meet Patents: The Economics of SEPs and FRAND

detail.abstract: Standards create value by enabling interoperability, network effects, and scale—but when implementing a standard requires patented technology, licensing becomes a distinctive bargaining problem. This article explains how standard-essential patents (SEPs) transform negotiations by creating lock-in and complementarity, motivating disputes over “hold-up” and “hold-out.” It then reviews the main governance responses: FRAND commitments that aim to anchor royalties to ex-ante incremental value, limits on injunction leverage, and coordination mechanisms such as patent pools. Finally, it explains why noisy, self-declared essentiality inflates thickets, complicates pooling, and raises transaction costs—highlighting the policy trade-off between rewarding contributions and preserving diffusion.

title: The Problem of Rulemaking in Uncertain Patent Markets - A Sociological Analysis of Patenting Strategies as a Device to Signal and Coordinate on the Rules of the Game
affiliations: George Mason University - Interdisciplinary Center for Economic Science

detail.title: The Problem of Rulemaking in Uncertain Patent Markets - A Sociological Analysis of Patenting Strategies as a Device to Signal and Coordinate on the Rules of the Game

declarations.funderStatement: A Swedish Research Council Grant

keywords: Signaling and Rules of the Game

detail.abstract:
This paper discusses the sociological implications of irreducible ex-ante uncertainty in patent markets. One can break down the firms' management of uncertainty in two sequential steps and characterize the first step as a sociological process where firms must define the rules of the game within which in the second stage economically efficient exchange can take place. Firms cannot explicitly coordinate/collude but can use patenting strategies (patent rights assets) as a device to signal and coordinate on the rules of the game. Through qualitative interviews I identify the types of signalling strategies and the conditions of exchange that derive from those. Four types of strategies were discovered – staying clear – strategic alignment – marginal transactions – systemic abuse – which all result in mutually assured self-restraint not to sue nor harm. The strategies thus result in socially strategic equilibriums (cooperative or non- cooperative) enabling (or blocking) markets with competitive equilibriums. Market prices thus exist given the strategies used to manage uncertainty given the formal (rules based) or informal (norms based) institutional constraints. The costs of operating a market therefore need to include the assets, i.e., the firms’ balance sheets, to create the socially strategic equilibriums, as well as transaction costs, i.e., the firms’
income statements. The firms organize after the strategies they pursue. Since all assets have some uncertainty, the findings provide elements to integrate uncertainty into economics. The standard economic theory is then a “special case” of the strategy space to manage uncertainty

title: A Physical Audit Protocol for GCC Sovereign AI Assets: Sovereign Compute Cannot Exceed Its Weakest Interconnect

detail.title: A Physical Audit Protocol for GCC Sovereign AI Assets: Sovereign Compute Cannot Exceed Its Weakest Interconnect

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author maintains no equity positions or commercial affiliations with cloud service providers, semiconductor manufacturers, advanced packaging houses, defense contractors, EPC contractors, or liquid cooling solution providers.
