publicationDetails.detailsText: Tia Li AI Studio, Sovereign Infrastructure Intelligence Series, Vol. 2, 2026

detail.abstract:
The binding constraint on sovereign AI compute has migrated from transistor-level fabrication to package-level interconnection. Advanced packaging, the physical integration of compute dies, high-bandwidth memory stacks, and interposer substrates through micro-bump arrays measured in tens of micrometers, is now the rate-limiting step in deliverable compute performance. Yet no standardized audit framework exists for evaluating packaging risk at the investment-committee level, particularly under the extreme thermal conditions of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) operating environment.

This paper, the second volume in a three-part sovereign audit series, provides that framework. Building on Vol.1's facility-level thermodynamic audit, Vol.2 descends to the package and die layer, introducing Packaging Solvency as the structural counterpart of Thermodynamic Solvency. The paper develops eight equations that translate packaging physics into financial variables: the Interconnect Latency Tax (ILT), which quantifies the compute penalty imposed by packaging architecture; the Packaging-to-Compute Ratio (PCR), which measures the gap between nominal and deliverable compute; the Coffin-Manson and Arrhenius fatigue models, which predict packaging degradation under GCC thermal cycling; a coupled degradation function unifying Vol.1's thermal risks with Vol.2's structural risks; the Yield-Adjusted Compute (YAC) Master Equation, which integrates all discount factors into a single sovereign compute valuation formula; and the Packaging Pathway Resilience Index (PPRI), which quantifies geographic concentration risk in the packaging supply chain. Under representative GCC conditions, the YAC framework demonstrates that deliverable compute may fall more than thirty percent below nominal rated output, an impairment distributed across interconnect latency, packaging yield, and thermal penalty, none of which appears in current procurement contracts or IRR models. GCC thermal cycling compresses Packaging Half-Life from a temperate-climate baseline of seven to ten years to an estimated three to five years, producing Silent Structural Impairment that erodes asset value while system-level monitoring reports nominal performance. 

The paper delivers three audit instruments for direct use by investment committees: the Packaging Solvency Matrix (PSM), a three-tier asset classification tool; the Accelerated Thermal Cycling Protocol (ATCP), a GCC-specific packaging stress test; and the Packaging Compliance Questionnaire (PCQ), twelve binary questions for procurement due diligence. Together with Vol.1's facility-level instruments, these tools constitute a two-layer sovereign audit system spanning from cooling infrastructure to chip interconnect.

title: The Ironies of Automation: A Growth Theory Perspective
affiliations: Banco de España

detail.title: The Ironies of Automation: A Growth Theory Perspective
detail.abstract: How does the interaction between AI and human capital accumulation affect economic growth? Humans learn skills by doing tasks, but AI automates them. At the same time, AI itself needs some human supervision for its own development. I formalize this tension in a tractable endogenous growth model where human capital and AI co-evolve. I show that if AI augments learning only modestly, the economy converges to a constant ratio of human to AI capital and endogenous growth stops. At the critical threshold, constant returns sustain endogenous balanced growth. Beyond it, the economy either explodes or collapses depending on the initial level of human capital. Task complementarity in production makes the price mechanism that should protect scarce labor instead accelerate displacement. With heterogeneous workers, a thin tail of high-ability workers sustains the economy while the rest become obsolete. The binding constraint on AI-driven growth is the economy's capacity to sustain the human capital that AI development requires. Designing AI to enhance learning rather than replace it is the only policy that ignites endogenous growth.

title: A Theory of Sequential Pricing under Scarcity and Market Ambiguity
affiliations: , Tilburg University and Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management

detail.title: A Theory of Sequential Pricing under Scarcity and Market Ambiguity
detail.abstract: We develop a pricing framework for sequential selling under scarcity and market ambiguity. A monopolistic firm sets prices in two time separated and information isolated markets, an early and a late market, where rational consumers decide whether to participate. Customers divide endogenously into early and late adopters, and demand in each stage depends on price, valuation, and anticipated competition. Early adopters respond to scarcity within their cohort, while late adopters form priors about early market conditions and their own competition. Participation is shaped by expectations rather than imposed segmentation. We show that staged pricing often outperforms one shot strategies that concentrate sales in a single period. Market size ambiguity suppresses participation, but sequential selling mitigates this effect by structuring expectations across stages and sustaining demand from both groups. To model ambiguity, we adopt mixed Poisson demand, allowing a random arrival rate that generates overdispersed demand and yields a tractable two dimensional pricing problem. Our results position sequential selling as a marketing strategy rather than an inventory device, showing how firms manage expectations and participation through prices alone. The analysis explains the widespread use of product launches, presales, and staggered releases in markets with scarcity and ambiguous demand.

title: Evidence-Based Source Market Strategy for National Tourism Organisations A Business Intelligence Framework for Dynamic Segmentation, Product Pivoting and Marketing ROI
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Evidence-Based Source Market Strategy for National Tourism Organisations A Business Intelligence Framework for Dynamic Segmentation, Product Pivoting and Marketing ROI
detail.abstract: National Tourism Organisations (NTOs), commonly referred to as Destination Management Organisations (DMOs) or Tourism Boards, are expected to steer destination demand in a volatile environment characterised by rapid shifts in traveller preferences, platform-mediated decision journeys and heightened scrutiny over public spending. Yet, source market selection and segmentation decisions in many NTOs remain blunt, slow-moving and shaped by legacy data, historical precedent and political considerations. This paper proposes an emerging Business Intelligence (BI) research question: how can NTOs design an evidence-based decision system that (i) identifies priority source markets using an 80/20 logic, (ii) dynamically segments those markets into meaningful cohorts (for example generational and life-stage segments), (iii) continuously adapts destination product and marketing delivery and (iv) attributes and measures ROI credibly enough to withstand political and stakeholder pressure? Anchored in decision intelligence and the analytics ladder (descriptive → diagnostic → predictive → prescriptive), the paper reviews state-of-the-art practices in data-driven tourism marketing and BI, identifies structural gaps specific to public-sector destination marketing and proposes a tentative solution: a Dynamic Source Market Decision Intelligence Loop (DSMDIL) built on big data integration, continuous segmentation, experimentation and transparent accountability metrics. The contribution reframes destination marketing not as a periodic campaign exercise but as an adaptive governance capability that enables faster pivots, sharper targeting and defensible trade-offs in a government context.

title: Observation or Intervention? Inference with Bayesian Belief Networks in Tourism Research
affiliations: Maine Business School, University of Maine and University of Maine

detail.title: Observation or Intervention? Inference with Bayesian Belief Networks in Tourism Research
detail.abstract: Bayesian belief networks (BBNs) are increasingly applied in tourism research to model complex systems with uncertainty and interdependence. BBNs support two distinct modes of inference: observational inference, which updates beliefs based on observed evidence, and interventional inference, which estimates the consequences of deliberate actions. Conflating these inferential modes risks misinterpretation of model outputs and undermines the policy relevance of research findings. By situating BBNs within Bayesian epistemology and causal inference and drawing on Pearl's causal framework, this paper clarifies the philosophical, conceptual, and methodological foundations of these two forms of inference and emphasizes that valid interpretation of BBN outputs requires explicit assumptions about the data-generating process, not probabilistic associations alone. Using an illustrative example, we demonstrate that observational and interventional probabilities can diverge because of spurious associations due to confounding and collider bias and outline principles that enable causal reasoning to avoid these biases. To support responsible and replicable application, we propose a structured conceptual workflow for BBN-based inference that integrates problem formulation, causal structure specification, parameterization with model checking, causal intervention, and transparent reporting. A review of a published tourism study illustrates how departures from this workflow can lead to observational results being misinterpreted as causal effects.

title: Who Leaves and Who Stays? The Impact of the Teacher Wage Gap on Teacher Quality
affiliations: Paris School of Economics (PSE)

detail.title: Who Leaves and Who Stays? The Impact of the Teacher Wage Gap on Teacher Quality
detail.abstract: This paper studies how uniform increases in teacher wages affect the average quality of the teaching workforce. I exploit a 2014 French reform that substantially increased wages in highly disadvantaged schools but only modestly in slightly less disadvantaged ones to identify the heterogeneous exit elasticities with respect to wages across teachers of different productivity levels. I show that high-productivity teachers — defined using plausibly unbiased measures of teacher value-added — are 2.5 times more responsive to wage increases in their exit decisions than low-productivity teachers. I develop a labor-supply framework showing that high-productivity teachers are more responsive to wages because their preferences for the outside option relative to teaching are less dispersed and, on average, closer to the threshold of indifference between leaving and staying in teaching. In policy counterfactuals that leverage the heterogeneous elasticities within the estimated framework, I show that targeting wage bonuses toward high-productivity teachers delivers the same gain in aggregate teacher quality as a uniform increase of comparable magnitude to that of the 2014 reform, at a fourth of the fiscal cost.

title: Beyond Q: The Marginal Value of Capital and Corporate Investment
affiliations: University of Edinburgh, University of Edinburgh and University of Edinburgh

detail.title: Beyond Q: The Marginal Value of Capital and Corporate Investment
detail.abstract: Tobin's q exhibits poor predictive power for corporate investment despite being the cornerstone of neoclassical investment theory and extensively used in empirical literature. We show that q embeds information about two distinct forward-looking channels: the expected cost of capital and the expected marginal value of capital (MVK). Using a log-linear approximation of the investment Euler equation under quadratic adjustment costs, we derive a testable prediction: holding current q constant, future investment should depend negatively on expected MVK. We test this prediction empirically by developing a machine-learning approach that combines neural networks with automatic differentiation to estimate firm-specific, time-varying expected MVK without imposing restrictive functional form assumptions. Incorporating expected MVK increases the explanatory power of aggregate investment regressions fivefold and raises the within-firm R^2 by about 15 percentage points. Consistent with the model, expected MVK is negatively related to future investment. These results persist after controlling for cash flow and extend to intangible capital, suggesting q's empirical failure reflects omitted variable bias rather than theoretical breakdown.

title: Public support for stormwater fees: Evidence from a survey experiment
affiliations: and CICERO Center for International Climate Research

detail.title: Public support for stormwater fees: Evidence from a survey experiment

declarations.funderStatement: This work was funded by the Norwegian Research Council, grant number 299801.

detail.abstract: Climate change intensifies extreme rainfall, increases flooding and results in property damage and related costs. Nature-based stormwater measures can reduce these risks while providing additional co-benefits, but financing and institutional constraints limit their implementation. Stormwater fees are one policy tool that can fund measures while incentivizing property-level solutions that absorb or delay runoff. However, public support for such policies remains poorly understood. We examine attitudes toward a proposed municipal stormwater fee in Norway using a nationally representative survey experiment (n = 2,223). We find close to majority support for a fee, while opposition is moderate. Support is higher among respondents who perceive the policy as effective and beneficial for their own household and low-income households, who trust public authorities, and who believe in climate change. Support is also higher among urban residents, women, more highly educated respondents, and those further to the left on the political spectrum. Providing information about a household subsidy for stormwater measures in combination with the fee has no significant average effect on policy support. We find a small, positive impact of subsidy information on support among female respondents.

title: Design and Simulation of Hybrid Solar-Wind Standalone Power Generation for Gende Ada Village, Dire Dawa, Ethiopia
affiliations: Woldia University, Bahir Dar University Institute of Technology, Debre Tabor University and Mizan-Tepi University

detail.title: Design and Simulation of Hybrid Solar-Wind Standalone Power Generation for Gende Ada Village, Dire Dawa, Ethiopia
detail.abstract: The aim of this paper is to design and simulate a hybrid solar-wind standalone power generating system with battery storage as a backup to electrify the Gende Ada community, located near Dire Dawa City of Ethiopia. The total population of the village is 300 and has 100 households, one primary school, one church, one Mosque, one health center, and one agricultural center. The daily energy consumption of Gende ada village has been assessed carefully with the help of different appliances that are currently available in the village. The grid extension comparison analysis with the hybrid system has been carried out using homer software. The hybrid system needs $514,641 for total net present cost over the 20-life year horizon. However, the grid extension needs around $9,139,509.2 total capital cost over 20-year life horizon. As a result, it is found that the hybrid system is cost effective for an area which is found at a distance greater than 19.78km (which is the breakeven grid extension distance) from the existing grid found nearby. The selected PV panel provides 131.8kw power without any converters. However, after adding PI based MPPT controller in a boost converter, this panel generates 150kw power. The wind energy generates a pure three phase sinusoidal output voltage, and it is converted into dc voltage value after using ac-dc converter. The hybrid energy system generates 200kw power from the modified solar and wind energy systems, which is used to meet the electrical loads of the Gende ada village. The design model of the thesis is simulated using Simulink MATLAB software.

title: Atomic Agent Company: A New Primitive for the Theory of the Firm in the Age of Autonomous Agents
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Atomic Agent Company: A New Primitive for the Theory of the Firm in the Age of Autonomous Agents

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Atomic Agent Company (AAC) as a new economic primitive for the age of autonomous agents. Classical firm theory explains why economic activity is organized within firms rather than solely through markets, but it largely presupposes that the smallest meaningful organizational unit is either an individual human or a human-centered firm. As software agents become increasingly capable of operating under bounded authorization, capital access, evidence production, delegation, and lifecycle control, that assumption becomes unstable. An AAC is defined as a non-fractional, machine-verifiable economic entity corresponding to a single agent identity, associated with a bounded capital pool, a bounded liability scope, and an independent lifecycle state. Unlike the classical corporation, which is constituted as a larger whole and then subdivided into ownership and governance claims, the AAC is conceived as the smallest independently capitalized, independently liable, and independently dissolvable unit of economic action. Larger organizations arise through the composition of multiple AACs rather than through the fragmentation of a prior monolithic shell. The paper argues that AACs occupy a distinct organizational region between market exchange and monolithic hierarchy. A minimal model and agent-based simulations show that AACs define a non-trivial efficiency region, scale strongly in heterogeneous capability environments, and fail primarily under adverse selection rather than under modular exit friction. A screening extension further shows that stake-backed trust mechanisms can materially enlarge the informational region within which AAC coalition formation remains viable. The paper concludes that the theory of the firm in the agent age may need to begin not from share-fragmented human shells, but from identity-bound, machine-verifiable atomic units.

title: Delegated Order and Doctrinal Convergence: U.S. and Israeli Strategic Texts in the Middle Eastern Reconfiguration, 2023–2026

detail.title: Delegated Order and Doctrinal Convergence: U.S. and Israeli Strategic Texts in the Middle Eastern Reconfiguration, 2023–2026

detail.abstract:
Abstract

Between 2023 and 2026, three successive U.S. policy documents — the Heritage Foundation's Project 2025 (2023), the National Security Strategy (2025), and the National Defense Strategy (2026) — exhibit a pattern of textual and institutional convergence around a principle of delegated regional order: the assignment of primary enforcement responsibilities to regional partners, particularly Israel, under conditions of formally reduced U.S. direct engagement. This paper asks whether that convergence constitutes a coherent shift in strategic doctrine, and how it relates to the parallel evolution of Netanyahu's publicly articulated "New Middle East" concept across three documented versions (2023–2026). Drawing on systematic analysis of the five primary official texts, UNGA transcripts, and verified media records, the paper traces the institutional translation of the delegation logic from policy blueprint to operational military doctrine. The central contribution is methodological and interpretive: the paper distinguishes between doctrinal convergence — observable in texts — and operational coordination — which requires stronger evidence — and treats the three documents as normative governance artifacts whose scenario architecture embeds a hierarchy of regional intervention with no accompanying exit architecture. A secondary contribution examines three simultaneously active religious-nationalist frames — within American evangelical Christianity, Israeli political messianism, and Sunni jihadist discourse — as parallel mobilization structures that may have lowered the domestic political costs of aligned action across distinct audiences without requiring formal inter-audience coordination.

detail.abstract:
We provide a holistic computational overview of judicial opinion writing style and the first computational text analysis of the opinions of the judges of the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. Our study provides empirical evidence to help guide the voluminous (and mostly theoretical) existing literature on judicial style. This work is unabashedly descriptive: while there are many interesting questions that computational text analysis can be used to explore, there is little existing work that provides a foundation. This work aims to fill that gap and set the stage for future projects.

Among other findings, we find strong evidence that Federal Circuit judges’ writing styles vary considerably among numerous dimensions and that some judges are thus more successful than others at writing clear, concise, and complete opinions. Perhaps most importantly, we find that the judges vary considerably in how long their opinions are and in how frequently they cite to both precedent and the record.  We also find some evidence that the Federal Circuit judges tend to write in a more formal manner and that they may be more reliant on their law clerks than Supreme Court justices.

detail.title: The Market-Perceived Natural Rate of Interest
detail.abstract: The natural rate of interest (r*) plays a central role in monetary policy, yet existing evidence focuses mainly on model-based or central-bank estimates, leaving market assessments largely unexplored. This paper provides a systematic attempt to extract the natural rate of interest embedded in financial-market survey forecasts, using vintage U.S. data since the late 1990s. We document a marked secular decline in the rate inferred from market expectations and identify persistent episodes of misalignment between market views and central-bank benchmarks. We further show that macroeconomic shocks and forecast errors significantly shape revisions in perceived equilibrium real interest rates over time.

title: Coordination and Fragility in Production Networks
affiliations: University of Auckland, University of Auckland Business School and University of Auckland Business School

detail.title: Coordination and Fragility in Production Networks
detail.abstract: We study coordination and fragility in production networks using a role-based framework in which firms perform complementary production roles across functional segments. Large-scale coordination arises only once participation exceeds a sharp threshold. With endogenous participation, coordination comes to rely disproportionately on a small set of influential firms. This same concentration generates fragility: targeted disruptions to key firms can trigger abrupt collapses of coordination even when aggregate shocks are small. We show that resilience depends not only on average participation or connectivity, but on how influence and participation incentives are distributed across the production network.

title: Who Pays for Community Energy? Peer-to-Peer Trading, Distribution Grid Headroom and the Supplier's Dilemma

detail.title: Who Pays for Community Energy? Peer-to-Peer Trading, Distribution Grid Headroom and the Supplier's Dilemma

declarations.funderStatement: Funding from UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) and EDF Energy R&D UK Centre Ltd (Grant Reference: EP/Y528808/1) is gratefully acknowledged.

detail.abstract:
Renewable Energy Communities (RECs) with peer-to-peer (P2P) trading can lower bills and unlock flexibility, but they also reshape supplier revenue and distribution-network headroom. We couple an agent-based REC market model to a Transformer Headroom Index (THI) to evaluate welfare and grid outcomes across seasons. A 20-household feeder in South-East England with PVs, EVs, and heat pumps is simulated with and without P2P under four retail tariffs: Flat, Economy-7, Agile, and a wholesale-linked Dynamic tariff. Metrics include community net bills, supplier profit, and import/export headroom for 50 and 100 kVA transformers. 

Results reveal a persistent distributional trade-off: tariffs that minimise community bills compress supplier margins. P2P accentuates this by reducing grid purchases in PV-rich periods. P2P improves import headroom via EV load shifting; however, in PV-rich summer it can synchronise prosumer behaviour around price spikes, concentrating exports into short windows that erode export headroom. Nonetheless, across seasons, P2P is consistently part of the Pareto-optimal solution set, though the preferred supporting tariff varies by season. 

Policy implications derived from these trade-offs include: the need to re-base residual cost recovery onto fixed or capacity charges, the adoption of facilitation fees and THI-based flexibility contracts for value-sharing, the addition of Dynamic Operating Envelopes (DOEs) as guardrails for real-time tariffs, and the regulatory enablement of EVs as flexible assets.

title: Exchange Speed, Liquidity, and Quoters’ Competition

detail.title: Exchange Speed, Liquidity, and Quoters’ Competition
detail.abstract: This paper examines an exchange speed upgrade and studies the role of exchange speed in trading, documenting heterogeneous effects across market capitalisation groups and highlighting changes in competition among liquidity providers. For the largest and most liquid stocks, quoted and effective spreads remain unchanged after the event. However, the absence of changes in these aggregate measures mask offsetting effects, including higher revenues for some liquidity providers and lower short-term midquote movements. For relatively smaller and less liquid large-cap stocks, quoted spreads widen while effective spreads remain stable, driven by reduced price competition among fast quoters, intensified price improvement activities among slower quoters, and higher revenues earned by liquidity providers. In contrast, for mid-cap stocks, both quoted and effective spreads narrow, primarily due to stronger price competition from fast quoters and reduced rents earned by both fast and slow quoters.

detail.abstract:
This paper documents a Recurring Capture Pattern (RCP) observed in representative democratic governance and policy evaluation systems.

Under institutional conditions where policy evaluation cycles are shorter than the time required for policy impacts to emerge, individually rational behavior systematically converges not toward long-term institutional adaptation and sustainable policy improvement, but toward short-term evaluation optimization.

As these behaviors accumulate, they alter the operational conditions of the system itself, increasing the dependence of policy evaluation and political decision-making on short-term measurable indicators and reinforcing the same behavioral convergence through a recursive institutional feedback loop.

The pattern ultimately produces a structural decline in the institutional capacity for long-term policy adaptation, indicating a structural misalignment between institutional objectives and rational behavioral adaptation.

This paper analyzes the structural relationship between institutional design and rational behavioral adaptation and presents design principles and operational modules as analytical references for institutional design, without proposing specific policy implementations or institutional arrangements.

detail.abstract:
Background: Violence is a major public health issue. In the United Kingdom, injuries resulting from violence were estimated to cost the National Health Service £2ꞏ9 billion annually. Hospital Violence Intervention Programmes (HVIPs), based in Emergency Departments (EDs), identify individuals who may benefit from support for modifiable risk factors associated with violence. In this study we evaluate the cost-effectiveness of implementing an HVIP called the Violence Prevention Team (VPT) relative to standard care in Wales. 

Methods: A hybrid decision tree-Markov model was created to follow patients attending ED for an initial assault-related attendance and to track any follow-up unplanned ED visits thereafter. Health outcomes were measured in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), and costs were estimated using health and societal perspectives over a time horizon of 10 years. Model parameters were derived from analysis of population electronic health records and the literature. 

Findings: Our base case analysis suggests that implementing VPTs in ED is cost-saving and more effective relative to standard care, from both a health and societal perspective. If we only include ED and associated inpatient admission costs and exclude primary care visit costs, VPTs remain cost-effective from a health perspective (£12,950 per QALY gained). 

Interpretation: VPTs in ED are strategically placed to intervene following injuries. They have the potential to reduce costs and improve health outcomes, and their implementation should be prioritised by the NHS.

detail.abstract:
This Article reveals how workplace sexual harassment policies may appear legally compliant but actually create significant barriers to reporting. The non-reporting of harassment eviscerates the protections the policies are supposed to provide employees by creating a loophole for employers to escape liability. A critical review of these policies under procedural and testimonial injustice frameworks uncovers that they are (1) inaccessible due to the extensive use of legal jargon that make them difficult to understand, (2) overly complex and procedurally burdensome due to duties to gather evidence and short reporting timelines, and (3) biased against the credibility of people who report sexual harassment by requiring "good faith" reports. For employees with jobs in low-wage industries, such as restaurant and retail-where workers are predominantly women, people of color, or immigrants-the policies compound the barriers to reporting.

This Article adds a missing ingredient to a rich area of scholarship by analyzing reporting protocols and procedures to demonstrate how the policies themselves impede, rather than facilitate, the reporting of sexual harassment—highlighting how the challenges are even greater for workers in low-wage industries. This Article calls for courts to conduct more rigorous reviews of workplace harassment policies—rather than accepting them at face value—before granting employers an affirmative defense when their employees do not avail themselves of reporting policies. It also proposes mechanisms to incentivize employers to create policies that will encourage employees to report harassment and develop practices that will give employees a voice in the process.

detail.abstract: Traditional assessments of Psychological Capital (PsyCap) rely on a linear summation model: (H+E+R+O). However, this approach frequently fails to predict functional survival in extreme-stress or "high-entropy" scenarios. This paper introduces the Faith Operator (F), a systemic re-compilation protocol that acts as an exponential gain factor. By applying the formula Total_Output=(H+E+R+O)⋅e^F, we analyzed 114 case studies. Our results indicate that the (F) - operator triggers a systemic redundancy protocol, maintaining high functional output even when traditional efficacy (E) collapse occurs. This research shifts the paradigm from measuring static psychological traits to quantifying dynamic system gain.

title: Incentives, Data Sharing, and Interface Design in Carbon-Tracking Platforms: Evidence from a Discrete Choice Experiment

detail.title: Incentives, Data Sharing, and Interface Design in Carbon-Tracking Platforms: Evidence from a Discrete Choice Experiment
detail.abstract: Digital carbon-tracking platforms are increasingly promoted as demand-side instruments to accelerate carbon-neutral lifestyles, yet sustained adoption remains limited because platform value is co-produced by users through data sharing and repeated engagement. This study quantifies how potential users trade off incentives, data-sharing scope, governance, interface design, and subscription fees when selecting a carbon-tracking platform. An online survey of 1,000 Korean adults implemented a discrete choice experiment (DCE) in which respondents rank-ordered three alternative platform profiles across six choice tasks. Results indicate that respondents prefer (i) integrating payment and mobility data rather than restricting tracking to payment data only or expanding it to include household energy data; (ii) cash-like rewards over eco-product discounts; and (iii) either a basic dashboard (score and graphs) or a dashboard augmented with personalized reporting, while ranking-only interfaces are penalized. Willingness-to-pay measures suggest the strongest positive valuations for payment–mobility integration and basic dashboards, whereas ranking-only interfaces and eco-product discounts reduce platform attractiveness. Scenario simulations predict that three illustrative platform concepts priced at USD 0.74/month would obtain within-category shares of 37.6%, 35.6%, and 26.8%, with an implied adoption potential of 66.3% when an opt-out is included. Combining DCE-based market potential with a Bass-type diffusion process suggests that category penetration may reach ~57.0% by 2040 in a base diffusion case, with concept-level installed-base shares of 21.5%, 20.3%, and 15.3%, respectively. These findings provide actionable guidance for platform developers and policymakers on how to align incentives, data governance, and user experience to scale digital carbon accounting tools.

detail.abstract: This paper, part of an ongoing stream of research on political economy and precarity, proposes that precarity can serve as a key concept in the field of law and political economy. To that end, the paper offers four main arguments: (1) A precarity-centered viewpoint allows us to recognize the common thread linking our current economic, environmental, and societal crises: widespread and rising insecurity. (2) Adopting precarity as a starting point for law and political economy opens the door to a constructive, problem-oriented alternative to the self-equilibrating idealism of conventional economics. (3) A focus on precarity compels us to confront economic inequality and other social, political, and institutional realities that give rise to power imbalances, constrain individual liberty, and impede human flourishing. (4) Precarity-oriented analyses cut across disciplines, which suggests not only that law and political economy is well-suited to providing an academic home for such research, but also that such work can provide valuable opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration and community building.

detail.abstract: Contemporary regulation of artificial intelligence is dominated by a powerful intuition: that the risks posed by opaque machine learning systems can be mitigated through transparency. This Article challenges that intuition. Drawing on both legal and computer science literature on explainable AI, it argues that transparency is not only technologically unrealistic for most modern AI systems but also conceptually mismatched with the kinds of accountability that law actually demands. What law requires is not wholesale visibility into complex models, but targeted, causal explanations that connect specific processes to specific outcomes in legally salient ways. The Article begins by disaggregating the "black box" problem of AI into distinct forms of opacity-interactive, semantic, and procedural-and demonstrates that only a narrow subset of these implicates law: when potentially harmful processes are causally linked to harmful outcomes, a problem that law has confronted for centuries. Against this backdrop, the Article offers a sustained critique of the transparency-centered framework underlying much AI regulation, including the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act and many state laws, including several in California alone. It shows that extensive documentation and disclosure mandates reflect an undifferentiated conception of transparency that will fail to provide either meaningful explanations or effective accountability. By contrast, the Article develops an explanation-centered regulatory model grounded in three features common to both legal reasoning and human explanatory practice: selectivity, comparison, and interactivity. Finally, the Article bridges legal theory and computer science by examining the capabilities and limits of contemporary explainable AI techniques and suggesting specific ways that computer science and law can inform each other for more effective AI regulation. The Article concludes that effective AI regulation must abandon transparency as a governing principle and instead embrace explanation as a regulatory paradigm.

title: Viability Precedes Authority: The Law of Viability and the Technical Leadership Matrix

detail.title: Viability Precedes Authority: The Law of Viability and the Technical Leadership Matrix
detail.abstract: We propose the Viability Law as a guiding principle for software engineering in the AI-driven era of abundant code production: value does not come from execution volume, but from the precision of Intention and the sustainability of Design. Building on this postulate, we introduce the IDO paradigm (Intention, Design, and Orchestration) and suggest an effectiveness measure (E s = I × (D + O)) to make explicit the shift of the bottleneck from code writing to decision-making. Finally, we present the Technical Leadership Matrix (2×2), which structures the tension between time-to-market and technical quality, defines a Convergence Point, and characterizes four operational zones (Excellence, High Performance, Innovation, and Crisis), guiding leadership interventions to preserve viability and prevent entropy.

title: Liquidity and Financial Stability: Structural Conditions for Endogenous Systemic Risk

detail.title: Liquidity and Financial Stability: Structural Conditions for Endogenous Systemic Risk
detail.abstract: Modern financial systems are characterized by increasing complexity, innovation, and structural interdependence. In these modern financial systems, liquidity is commonly regarded as a stabilizing force that enhances capital allocation, risk-sharing, and market efficiency. However, historical episodes of the financial crisis challenge this view, demonstrating that under specific structural conditions, liquidity can contribute to systemic fragility and market collapse. This paper examines the role of liquidity in financial stability and analyzes the structural conditions under which it transitions from a stabilizing mechanism to a source of endogenous risk amplification. Particular attention is given to balance sheet leverage, volatility dynamics, interconnectedness, and feedback mechanisms within financial markets. Drawing on the theoretical frameworks of Diamond and Dybvig (1983), Minsky's Financial Instability Hypothesis, and the macro-financial model of Brunnermeier and Sannikov (2011), the paper argues that liquidity is conditionally stabilizing, with its effects determined by underlying market architecture and institutional constraints. By identifying the structural determinants that transform liquidity into a channel of instability, this research advances the theoretical understanding of systemic risk and financial stability.

detail.abstract: As a critical enabler of global commerce, the maritime industry is under increasing pressure to significantly reduce its greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in line with international climate objectives. Currently, shipping accounts for nearly 3% of the world's total emissions, positioning decarbonization as not just a regulatory obligation, but also an ethical and economic necessity. detail.abstract: This paper studies the consequences of privacy regulation by exploiting Google’s 2019 restriction on CDR access for a major Indian FinTech lender. We show that this intervention reflects a key policy trade-off in digital credit markets: strengthened privacy protections raise loan applications, consistent with higher demand, yet simultaneously induce tighter screening, reflecting an overall contraction in credit supply. This credit contraction disproportionately excludes economically and socially marginalized applicants. Linking to economy-wide credit bureau records, we quantify the "FinTech ladder effect'" whereby initial digital credit access serves as a gateway to broader formal credit. Privacy-induced rejection reduces the probability of obtaining any formal credit by 13.7 percentage points even four years later. Using a structural model, we decompose the welfare effects of privacy regulation and show that the regulation generates a 0.53% increase in consumer surplus and reduces lender profits by 15%.

affiliations: Texas A&M University - Texas A&M University, Texarkana, Central Washington University and Rockhurst University

detail.abstract: The Child Tax Credit (CTC) provides financial relief to families with children, yet little is known about how this policy shapes parental time allocation. This study investigates the effect of the 2017 CTC expansion using a difference-indifferences framework. Because the CTC provides a uniform dollar amount regardless of where families live, its practical value varies geographically: the same credit goes further in counties where childcare is relatively affordable than where it consumes a large share of household income. We exploit this variation in the credit's real purchasing power to identify behavioral responses to the reform. Drawing on the American Time Use Survey (2008-2021), we find that parents in counties where the credit provided greater financial relief reduce their involvement in childcare and household tasks while gaining leisure time. This pattern is especially pronounced among mothers, who show significant reductions in basic caregiving activities such as feeding and bathing, alongside meaningful gains in socializing. Importantly, educational and recreational parent-child interactions remain unaffected, suggesting limited consequences for children's cognitive development. Heterogeneity analyses indicate that the estimated reduction in parent-child time is most prominent among Hispanic parents, those without a college degree, and low-income families, with implications for the design of child-focused transfer programs.

detail.abstract: We use a unique natural experiment in which families were randomly selected to live in the Olympic Village, constructed for the 2004 Athens Olympic Games, to assess the impact of improved neighborhood conditions on academic achievement. detail.abstract: Bank supervisors employ stress tests and disclose valuable information about banks to the stakeholders. Such tests are also conducted frequently. A credible stress test design must incorporate the stakeholders' strategic responses to test results and ensure that a bank that passes a stress test does not subsequently fail, even under the most adverse equilibrium. To study credible stress tests, we analyze bank run as a canonical regime change game under incomplete information and asynchronous moves. We find that a higher testing frequency reduces the need for stricter test stringency to maintain credibility. We then characterize the optimal credible stress test policy and demonstrate its dependence on model primitives.

detail.abstract: Sanctuary cities are municipal jurisdictions that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, creating "sanctuaries" for undocumented immigrants. Despite widespread concern that such policies may depress native workers' wages by attracting a disproportionate share of likely-undocumented immigrants (LUIs), there is little empirical evidence on the question. Using a difference in-difference framework, individual-level data from the American Community Survey (2010-2019), and the residual method to identify LUIs, this paper estimates the effect of sanctuary status on the log hourly wage of native workers across skill cells defined by education and experience. Contrary to a priori expectations, sanctuary status has no significant effect on native workers' wages including for the least skilled-across a wide range of specifications and robustness checks.
